headline: Migrants' Money Home Nearly Doubles in a Decade

summary_short: Migrants sent $728.6 billion home to families in 2025, nearly double the amount from a decade earlier, according to the UN's International Fund for Agricultural Developm…
body:
Migrants sent $728.6 billion home to families in low and middle-income countries in 2025—nearly double the amount recorded a decade earlier, according to the UN's International Fund for Agricultural Development. Between 2016 and 2025, remittances grew by 94 percent, far outpacing the 28 percent increase in the number of migrants from those countries. This gap reveals something encouraging: the growth reflects not just more people migrating, but migrants abroad sending larger amounts home. An estimated 220 million migrants and diaspora members now support 1.1 billion relatives, typically sending $300 to $400 nine or ten times a year. These private family transfers exceed global official development assistance and foreign direct investment to low and middle-income countries combined.

The impact is most visible where it matters most. In Honduras, remittances equaled 30 percent of GDP in 2025; in El Salvador, 28 percent. Latin America and the Caribbean saw the fastest growth, rising 132 percent to $168.6 billion. Yet this reliance also carries risk. Research shows 61 percent of returnees surveyed in Guatemala had been their household's main income earner, meaning deportations or employment restrictions abroad can devastate families left behind.

How families use the money tells a deeper story. Three-quarters covers immediate needs—food, shelter, utilities. The remaining quarter funds healthcare, education, housing, savings, and small businesses. Nearly a third of all remittances, around $233 billion, reached rural economies in 2025, where financial services and jobs remain scarce. Families also invest an estimated $22 billion annually in rural agriculture. As climate disasters increase, remittances increasingly help households replace lost income and rebuild. Yet experts stress these private resources cannot replace public investment in social protection and climate finance.
